   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?

Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Medtronic is a top-dog medtech incumbent rather than a Rule Breaker: it leads mature device markets but entered the fastest-growing ones (pulsed-field ablation, surgical robots) as a follower. Its stock has lagged for five years and few commentators call it overvalued, so it shows few of Gardner's six traits.
summaries.buffett: It is an understandable business with durable franchises, 49 straight years of dividend increases and $5.4B of FY2026 free cash flow, which Buffett would like. Against that, returns on capital are modest (ROIC about 8.6%) because of the $43B of goodwill from Covidien, and a decade of retained earnings produced little growth in shareholder value.
summaries.munger: Munger would see a sensible, hard-to-kill franchise with regulatory and switching-cost moats, but not a great compounding business: GAAP EPS grew only from $2.48 in FY2016 to $3.73 in FY2026. At about 16 times forward earnings it is a fair-price, decent business rather than the wonderful business he sought.
summaries.lynch: Medtronic fits Lynch's stalwart category: a large, steady company growing sales mid-to-high single digits (8.4% in FY2026, 7.25%-7.75% organic guided for FY2027). With a forward P/E near 16 against roughly 8% EPS growth, it is not cheap on his P/E-to-growth test, but a turn in growth from PFA and Hugo could make it a modest stalwart winner.
summaries.fisher: Fisher would credit the steady stream of new products (Affera PFA, Micra, Inceptiv, Hugo; more than 315 major-market approvals in FY2026) and a huge global sales force. He would question R&D productivity at only 7.9% of sales and the reliance on acquisitions, and long-run margins have not risen.
summaries.graham: Medtronic passes Graham's tests for size, unbroken profits and dividends (49 consecutive increases) and EPS growth over ten years (+50%). It fails on price: about 28 times three-year average GAAP EPS and a P/E times P/B product well above 22.5.
summaries.thiel: Medtronic is not a Zero-to-One monopoly: it competes in oligopolies with Abbott, Boston Scientific, J&J and Edwards, and its technology is not ten times better than rivals'. Its strengths are distribution and durability rather than proprietary breakthroughs.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth, efficiency and a reasonable price; Medtronic's Elliott-prompted push to cut costs, separate MiniMed and focus on growth areas fits his 'get fit' theme. However, revenue growth plus free-cash-flow margin is about 23%, well short of the profiles he favours.
summaries.druckenmiller: Recent fundamentals are improving: Q1 FY2027 revenue rose 13.7% (helped by an extra week), guidance was raised and the stock recovered from about $81 in April 2026 to $94.75. But it is a defensive, low-beta (0.57) medtech name without the macro or liquidity tailwind or high-conviction story Druckenmiller typically concentrates in.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high returns on capital, high gross margins and growth; Medtronic has the 65% gross margin and cash conversion but ROIC near 8.6% and slow growth over the past decade. It would likely fall below his quality bar despite a sensible price.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Medtronic looks mediocre: operating profit of $6,467M is about 4.8% of a roughly $135B enterprise value, and return on tangible capital is held down by heavy debt. It would not rank near the top of his screens.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a great business, talented owner-minded management and reinvestment opportunities; Medtronic is a good but not exceptional business, has hired-manager leadership and reinvests at only high-single-digit returns. It fits the stool only partly.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks simple, distressed businesses with heads-I-win odds; Medtronic is simple and unlikely to suffer permanent loss, but it is not distressed or deeply cheap, so the upside-versus-downside asymmetry he looks for is limited.
summaries.wood: Medtronic is not a disruptive-innovation leader in ARK's sense: its robotics (Hugo) and AI efforts (GI Genius, Touch Surgery) are challengers to stronger incumbents, and its cost curves are not falling sharply. Cathie Wood would see it as an incumbent at risk of disruption rather than a disruptor.
summaries.ackman: Ackman likes simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with high barriers to entry; Medtronic fits much of that, and Elliott's 2025 stake shows it can attract activist interest. The questions are its modest growth and returns, which an activist case would aim to improve through portfolio focus.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep looked for scale economies shared with customers; Medtronic's scale mostly funds trials and sales forces and is not passed back as lower prices, so it is not a classic Nomad-style business. Its position is durable but not clearly strengthening year by year.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed companies attacking huge new markets with great technology; Medtronic is a mature incumbent founded in 1949, so his venture lens fits only its new businesses such as Hugo and renal denervation.
summaries.nash: Medtronic fails several of Nash's instant-kill and scoring tests: debt exceeds cash, GAAP operating margin is 17.8% (below 20%), and revenue growth is below 10% (8.4% in FY2026). Its DCF value under his method is below the $94.75 share price even before using a 12% discount rate, so it scores well below his 75-point bar.

momentum.evidence: The stock rose from about $81 at the end of April 2026 to $94.75 on Oct 16, 2026, but it is roughly flat over the past year (-0.6%), lagging the market.

g4.evidence: Geoff Martha is a competent operator, and Elliott Management took a large stake in August 2025, after which Medtronic added two independent directors and formed portfolio and operating committees; it is not backed by famous growth investors as partners.

g6.evidence: Commentators generally describe Medtronic as cheap or fairly valued (forward P/E about 16, Barclays Equal Weight with a $95 target in October 2026), not overvalued.

simple.evidence: It makes and sells medical devices such as pacemakers, heart valves, spine implants and surgical tools to hospitals, a business a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: It has been profitable for decades and raised its dividend for 49 consecutive years, but revenue only rose from $28,833M in FY2016 to $36,364M in FY2026 and fell in FY2023.

integrity.evidence: Reporting is candid and audited by PwC, but heavy non-GAAP adjustments ($5.53 non-GAAP versus $3.73 GAAP EPS in FY2026) and past capital allocation (the $50B Covidien deal) have drawn activist criticism.

b6.evidence: It has pruned the portfolio (exiting ventilators and separating MiniMed in October 2026), but its history includes the empire-building Covidien acquisition and a steady stream of tuck-in deals.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 8.6% and ROE about 10.7%, held down by $43,187M of goodwill and $28,153M of debt.

fcf.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow was $5,426M (operating cash flow $7,330M minus $1,904M capex), more than GAAP net income of $4,801M.

b10.evidence: GAAP EPS rose only 50% from $2.48 in FY2016 to $3.73 in FY2026 and the share price ($94.75) is below where it was five years ago (about $120 in October 2021), so retained earnings have not created matching value.

safety.evidence: A DCF using 3-year average growth (5.2%) and FCF margin (15.5%) gives about $68 per share at a 10% discount rate, below the $94.75 price.

fairprice.evidence: At about 16 times forward non-GAAP EPS and a roughly 4.7% FCF yield it is reasonably priced for a mid-single-digit grower, but not cheap on GAAP earnings (trailing P/E about 23).

mu5.evidence: With dozens of product lines, about 150 countries and long-term implant relationships, the main failure risks are large recalls, debt or poor capital allocation rather than obsolescence.

reinvest.evidence: It reinvests about $2.9B a year in R&D and buys growth assets such as Affera and CathWorks, but returns on that capital have been only high single digits.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic stalwart: a large, slow-growing, dividend-paying company whose story is a pickup in growth from PFA, renal denervation and Hugo.

ly3.evidence: The forward P/E of about 16 is roughly twice its expected EPS growth of about 8% (FY2027 non-GAAP EPS guidance $5.94-$6.00 versus $5.53).

runway.evidence: Ageing populations and new markets (pulsed-field ablation, hypertension, robotic surgery) support mid-to-high single-digit growth for years, but not substantial multi-fold expansion.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 1,354.0M in FY2021 to 1,288.1M in FY2026 and 55,032,401 shares were retired in the October 2026 MiniMed exchange offer, but insiders own only about 0.04% and there is no notable insider buying.

ly8.evidence: It is covered by about 30 analysts and held about 91% by institutions.

fi2.evidence: It keeps launching next-generation products, including Affera Sphere-9 and Sphere-360 PFA catheters, Hugo (FDA-cleared for urology in December 2025, filed for general and gynecologic surgery in June 2026) and the Inceptiv closed-loop spinal cord stimulator.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $2,873M (7.9% of FY2026 sales) produced more than 315 major-market approvals, but several of its fastest-growing products came from acquisitions.

fi4.evidence: Its global sales and clinical-support force reaches hospitals in about 150 countries, which is why Cardiac Ablation Solutions could grow 78% in Q4 FY2026 after launch.

longterm.evidence: It keeps funding long-term programmes such as Hugo and renal denervation, but its large dividend and cost-cutting under activist pressure show strong attention to near-term returns.

gr1.evidence: It had $36,364M of FY2026 revenue and a market value of about $116B.

ni10.evidence: GAAP net income was positive in every year from FY2016 ($3,538M) through FY2026 ($4,801M).

gr4.evidence: The FY2027 dividend increase to $2.88 a year was its 49th consecutive annual increase.

eps10.evidence: GAAP diluted EPS rose from $2.48 in FY2016 to $3.73 in FY2026, up 50%.

gr6.evidence: The price of $94.75 is about 28 times average GAAP EPS of $3.37 over FY2024-FY2026.

gr7.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 23 times a price-to-book of about 2.3 gives roughly 54, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its devices are competitive but not ten times better than rivals' such as Boston Scientific's Farapulse, Abbott's AVEIR or Intuitive's da Vinci.

timing.evidence: Timing is good for PFA and renal denervation (permanent CPT codes from 2028), but late for robotics, where Intuitive has a two-decade head start.

th3.evidence: It grew from pacemakers in 1957 into a broad conglomerate largely through acquisitions such as Covidien, not a Thiel-style small-market monopoly expansion.

team.evidence: Management under Geoff Martha and CFO Thierry Piéton is experienced, but it is not a founder-led or widely acclaimed world-class team.

th5.evidence: Its hospital contracts, clinical specialists and sales force in about 150 countries are a major distribution advantage.

durable.evidence: Implantable cardiac, neuro and spine franchises protected by clinical data, FDA approvals and surgeon training are likely to remain relevant for 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Its growth bets (PFA, robotics, renal denervation) are markets competitors also see and pursue.

trend.evidence: It benefits from the ageing-population and minimally invasive-procedure trends, but is not a leading beneficiary of a platform shift such as AI.

dr1.evidence: Revenue growth accelerated from 3.6% in FY2025 to 8.4% in FY2026 and 13.7% in Q1 FY2027, and FY2027 guidance was raised to 7.25%-7.75% organic growth and $5.94-$6.00 EPS.

dr2.evidence: After the MiniMed separation and with PFA, Hugo and Symplicity ramping, the company could look leaner and faster-growing in 18-24 months, though much of this is already discussed by analysts.

dr4.evidence: Lower interest rates would ease its $28.2B debt burden and support defensive dividend stocks, but tariffs and hospital budget pressures work against it.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include FDA decisions on Hugo for general and gynecologic surgery, PFA share gains, renal-denervation reimbursement and post-MiniMed cost cuts.

dr7.evidence: Growth, returns on capital and the DCF valuation do not support a large, concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin (excluding amortization) was 65.0% in FY2026, though down from 68.0% in FY2022.

fcfyield.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow of $5,426M on a market value of about $116B is a yield of about 4.7%, reasonable for mid-single-digit growth.

gb2.evidence: FY2026 operating profit of $6,467M is only about 4.8% of an enterprise value of about $135B.

pa2.evidence: The FY2023 revenue dip and margin squeeze from inflation and tariffs look fixable and growth has returned, but slower structural growth is not a temporary setback.

pa4.evidence: With $5.4B of annual free cash flow, interest covered about 9x and essential devices, the chance of permanent loss of capital is small.

wo1.evidence: It has robotics (Hugo) and AI products (GI Genius, Touch Surgery) but is not a leader in those fields.

wo2.evidence: There is no sign of rapidly falling unit costs opening new demand; gross margin has declined.

wo3.evidence: It combines robotics, AI-assisted imaging and connected implants, but none at a leading or convergent scale.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable markets grow at mid-to-high single digits and are unlikely to be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Demand for life-saving procedures is defensive (beta 0.57), but tariffs, currency moves and $715M of annual net interest expense still affect results.

ns1.evidence: Medtronic does not pass scale savings to customers as falling prices; it uses scale to fund trials and sales coverage.

ns4.evidence: Its position should hold, and PFA and renal denervation could strengthen it, but it is not clearly stronger in 10-20 years given Intuitive and Boston Scientific's leads.

va2.evidence: Its devices treat heart failure, arrhythmias, chronic pain, stroke and other serious conditions for 82 million patients a year.

tn1.evidence: It sells into the ageing-population and minimally invasive-surgery trends but is an established company retrofitting into newer areas such as robotics and AI.

tn2.evidence: The market sees a slow, bloated conglomerate, while after the MiniMed separation it is reshaping toward faster cardiovascular growth (Cardiovascular grew 18.9% organically in Q1 FY2027), but it is not a transformation on the scale of Palantir or Tesla.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap, non-Chinese, non-commodity, non-seasonal company founded in 1949.

tn4.evidence: It passes two of three: revenue grew in FY2024-FY2026 and it is profitable ($4,801M FY2026 net income), but debt of $28,153M exceeds cash of $8,819M.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow is positive each quarter ($1,290M in Q1 FY2027), but debt has exceeded cash and investments at every recent quarter-end.

tn6.evidence: FY2026 revenue grew 8.4% (5.8% organic); Q1 FY2027's 13.7% was helped by a 53rd week worth about $570M.

tn7.evidence: FY2026 revenue growth of 8.4% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 14.9% is about 23, below 40.

tn8.evidence: In FY2026 revenue grew 8.43% while total operating costs grew 8.39% ($29,897M versus $27,582M), so only barely.

tn9.evidence: It triggers several instant kills: debt exceeds cash, GAAP operating margin was 17.8% in FY2026 (below 20%), and annual revenue growth is below 10%.

tn10.evidence: There is no existential legal threat, but recurring product-liability litigation (certain litigation charges of $113M in FY2026 and $317M in FY2025) and FDA oversight remain.

tn11.evidence: Medtronic provides implantable and surgical devices that help hospitals and doctors treat heart, nerve and surgical conditions, and charges per device and procedure kit; customers choose it for clinical evidence, breadth and support.

tn13.evidence: Total 65/130: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 5, short interest (3.3%) 10, institutional ownership (91%) 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 5, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell in FY2023, free cash flow did not rise steadily ($5,978M in FY2022 vs $4,580M in FY2023), and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 9x (FY2026 operating profit $6,467M / $715M interest), the current ratio is 2.07 and liabilities are 0.83x equity, but assets excluding goodwill ($50,119M) are only 1.18x liabilities ($42,456M).

tn18.evidence: Geoff Martha has delivered the fastest growth in 10 years in FY2026, but he has been CEO only since 2020, is not a founder and has no notable open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: Q4 FY2026 revenue and EPS came in ahead of guidance and expectations, and Q1 FY2027 beat estimates and led to a raised FY2027 outlook.

tn21.evidence: There is no clown CEO, co-CEO, fraud or auditor change (PwC), but gross margin has declined from 68.0% to 65.0% over four years and inventories rose to $6,215M in Q1 FY2027 from $5,951M.

tn22.evidence: It has $36.4B of revenue, steady profits, falls in share count rather than dilution, and little media hype.

tn24.evidence: Working back from $94.75 with a 15.5% FCF margin, a 10% discount rate and 4% terminal growth implies about 12% annual revenue growth for five years, above the 5.2% three-year average it has delivered.

tn25.evidence: Nash's DCF (5.2% growth, 15.5% FCF margin, 4% terminal growth, net debt of $19.3B, about 1,225M shares) gives about $47 per share at a 12% discount rate, well below $94.75.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E of about 16 is below large-cap medtech peers such as Boston Scientific and Stryker, but the PEG of roughly 2 (16 / about 8% EPS growth) is above 1.
